strengths: The paper introduces a mathematically grounded ADMM-based framework (SALAAD) to induce sparse and low-rank (SLR) structures during LLM pretraining, moving away from heuristic post-hoc or rigid layer-agnostic schedules.
The proposed I-controller is an elegant solution to adaptively adjust block-wise regularization thresholds during training, reducing the hyperparameter tuning search space to a single coefficient.

The Homomorphic Parameter Allocation (HPA) strategy enables smooth, continuous, and post-hoc adjustment of model capacities from a single training run, which is highly practical for elastic deployment.
The finding that embedding layers naturally exhibit a benign and stable SLR structure within this framework is insightful and challenges previous design choices that excluded them from compression.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations, thorough ablation studies, and comprehensive learning dynamics analyses.
weaknesses: Training-time memory and computational overhead is significant. SALAAD requires storing several surrogate components (L, S, and Y) in addition to original weights, and requires periodic SVD computations. Although the authors suggest parallelizing this across GPUs, it still adds engineering complexity and potential training bottlenecks.

There is a notable performance degradation when training in bfloat16 instead of float32 (as shown in Table 4 vs Table 1). Since large-scale LLM pretraining is heavily reliant on lower-precision formats like bfloat16 for speed and memory efficiency, this sensitivity to numerical precision is a limitation.

The baseline comparisons in Table 1 are slightly mismatched, as the baselines were trained in bfloat16 while the main SALAAD results are trained in float32. A more direct comparison under the same precision settings in the main text would strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: The paper proposes a mathematically principled formulation using ADMM to optimize a robust PCA objective (low-rank + sparse) directly during LLM pretraining, moving away from heuristics.

The block-wise I-controller is a clever design that adaptively regulates the rank and sparsity thresholds during training based on energy coverage and target density. This eliminates the need for tedious manual tuning of layer-wise hyperparameters.

The Homomorphic Parameter Allocation (HPA) strategy enables continuous, post-hoc model capacity adjustment in weight space. A single pretrained checkpoint can be dynamically scaled to meet various memory budgets without retraining.

The empirical observation and characterization of the structural asymmetry between different LLM submodules (specifically showing that embedding layers are highly SLR-inducible while LM heads are not) provides valuable new insights for structured compression.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks practical inference hardware benchmarks (e.g., actual GPU memory footprint and latency measurements). Since the model architecture uses a sum of a low-rank and a sparse component, executing this decomposition efficiently in GPU kernels can be challenging. Showing parameter counts alone does not guarantee real-world acceleration or memory savings during deployment.

The training overhead is not empirically benchmarked. Although Appendix B analyzes the theoretical FLOPs of block-wise SVD updates, the paper does not report actual training wall-clock time comparisons or training throughput against baselines. It is unclear how much the two-stage ADMM optimization slows down the pretraining loop.

The main results in Table 1 are trained in float32, which is highly impractical for standard LLM pretraining due to memory constraints. While the authors provide bfloat16 results in Appendix D, the main-text comparison would be stronger and more realistic if bfloat16 was the default setting throughout.

strengths: A principled optimization formulation based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) and augmented Lagrangian to induce sparse and low-rank (SLR) structures during LLM pretraining.

The introduction of an I-controller to adaptively and dynamically update block-wise thresholds (alpha, beta) based on global target compression objectives, eliminating manual layer-by-layer hyperparameter tuning.
The Homomorphic Parameter Allocation (HPA) strategy allows a single pretrained model to be continuously adjusted to different parameter budgets at deployment time without retraining.

Interesting empirical findings demonstrating that embedding layers can naturally adapt to SLR structures under the proposed framework without hurting training stability, unlike prior works that systematically excluded them.
Well-structured manuscript with detailed ablation studies on step sizes, penalty parameters, and allocation ratios.
weaknesses: High Training Complexity and Numerical Instability: The main SALAAD experiments require training in FP32 (float32) to maintain numerical stability, whereas modern LLM pretraining baselines are trained in BF16 (bfloat16). Appendix D shows that training SALAAD in BF16 leads to performance degradation, suggesting that the optimization is sensitive to precision and might not scale easily to standard mixed-precision pretraining pipelines.

Significant Training Memory Overhead: The proposed method requires storing auxiliary matrices L, S, and Y for each weight matrix X. This dramatically increases the memory footprint during training (tripling or quadrupling the model parameter state). While the authors suggest distributing these surrogate blocks across GPUs, doing so in practice with standard distributed training setups (e.g., FSDP, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, Tensor Parallelism) introduces significant engineering complexity and communication overhead.

Lack of Practical Inference Benchmarks: Despite 'Large Language Model Inference' being in the title, the paper does not provide actual hardware benchmarks (e.g., latency, throughput, memory usage during generation) for the sparse + low-rank models. Executing sparse and low-rank matrix multiplications simultaneously on modern hardware (like GPUs or edge devices) often suffers from low kernel efficiency and might not translate parameter savings into actual wall-clock speedups.

High Computational Overhead of SVD: Even though SVD updates are performed periodically (every K=40 steps), performing SVD on large matrices (e.g., 4096x4096 or larger) still introduces non-trivial overhead. For scale-up to larger models (e.g., 7B, 70B), the SVD step could become a severe bottleneck unless highly optimized GPU-parallelized solvers are used.

Unfair/Unclear Perplexity Comparison: The perplexity results in Table 1 compare SALAAD (trained in FP32) with baselines (trained in BF16). Since higher numerical precision typically improves perplexity, this gives SALAAD an unfair advantage in the comparison. Furthermore, the baseline LOST still outperforms SALAAD in several configurations.

strengths: Principled and mathematically sound formulation: Applying the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to induce sparse and low-rank (SLR) structures during pretraining provides a rigorous alternative to heuristic-based approaches.

Adaptive regularization via I-Controller: The introduction of an integral controller to dynamically adjust rank and sparsity thresholds (alpha, beta) block-by-block eliminates the need for labor-intensive, hand-crafted schedule tuning.

Elastic post-hoc deployment: The Homomorphic Parameter Allocation (HPA) strategy allows a single pretrained checkpoint to scale continuously across various parameter/memory budgets at deployment time without retraining.

Valuable structural insights: The discovery of SLR-inducibility asymmetry in LLM submodules (i.e., embedding layers exhibit benign SLR behavior, whereas the LM head does not) provides useful guidelines for structured pretraining.

Comprehensive empirical validation: SALAAD is evaluated across scales (60M to 1B parameters) and shows state-of-the-art compression-to-perplexity trade-offs compared to representative baselines like SLTrain and LOST.
weaknesses: High training-time computational overhead: Figure 2 indicates that the SVD computations in the ADMM stage introduce significant wall-clock training overhead (e.g., adding several thousand minutes of runtime for the 1B model), which may limit its practicality under tight pretraining compute budgets.

Lack of deployment-time hardware benchmarks: While the paper demonstrates param-count reduction, it does not present actual hardware measurements (e.g., GPU memory footprints, latency, or throughput speedups) when executing the sparse + low-rank format. Unstructured sparsity typically requires specialized kernel support to achieve real-world latency/memory benefits on standard hardware.

Sensitivity to training precision: The best performance is achieved using float32 training. When trained entirely in bfloat16 (Table 5), there is a moderate degradation in perplexity. Given that modern LLM pretraining heavily relies on low-precision formats (bfloat16/FP8) for throughput, this degradation is a notable limitation.

strengths: A principled formulation of sparse and low-rank (SLR) decomposition integrated into LLM pretraining using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM).
The introduction of an adaptive I-controller that dynamically adjusts block-wise rank and sparsity thresholds, successfully mitigating the need for manual per-layer hyperparameter tuning.
The Homomorphic Parameter Allocation (HPA) strategy enables a single trained model checkpoint to support continuous, elastic, and post-hoc capacity scaling in weight space without retraining.

An insightful empirical discovery regarding LLM component asymmetry under SLR, demonstrating that the embedding layers converge stably under adaptive SLR induction whereas the language modeling (LM) head does not.
weaknesses: High Training-Time Overhead: As illustrated in the wall-clock breakdown in Figure 2, SALAAD exhibits a severe training slowdown. For the 1B model, SALAAD takes roughly 5.6x longer to train compared to vanilla pretraining (increasing from ~800 to ~4500 minutes). This makes it highly impractical for actual large-scale LLM pretraining where training efficiency is a primary bottleneck.

Unfair/Inconsistent Comparison and Performance Degradation under bfloat16: The main results in Table 1 present SALAAD trained in float32 while the baselines are in bfloat16, giving SALAAD an unfair advantage. When compared under the standard bfloat16 training setting (Appendix E, Table 5), SALAAD's perplexity degrades and it underperforms existing baselines (e.g., for the 350M model, SALAAD bfloat16 gets 19.73 PPL compared to SLTrain's 19.42 PPL and LOST's 18.95 PPL under similar parameter budgets).

Increased Training Memory: Storing the auxiliary surrogate variables (L, S, Y) for each target block during training adds a non-trivial memory footprint, which can restrict the training batch size or require additional hardware resources.

strengths: Principled mathematical formulation using ADMM and an augmented Lagrangian framework to jointly optimize dense weights and structured sparse-plus-low-rank (SLR) surrogates during training.
Introduction of a block-wise adaptive I-controller to dynamically balance rank and sparsity thresholds, reducing the burden of manual hyperparameter tuning across heterogeneous model blocks.
Interesting empirical findings regarding the SLR-inducibility of different Transformer components, showing that embedding layers are highly amenable to SLR induction, whereas the LM head is not.
weaknesses: Unfair and misleading evaluation setup regarding training precision: In the main comparison (Table 1), SALAAD is trained in float32, whereas all baselines are trained in bfloat16. High-precision float32 training provides an unfair optimization and perplexity advantage. In Appendix E (Table 5), where SALAAD is trained in bfloat16, its performance degrades considerably (e.g., at 130M, the compressed model perplexity is 25.67, which is worse than the 24.05 of the LOST baseline). This precision discrepancy should be addressed and corrected in the main text.

Lack of actual inference latency and hardware deployment results: Despite having 'Large Language Model Inference' in the title, the paper does not provide any real-world inference speedup or GPU memory reduction benchmarks. Unstructured sparsity (induced by the l1-norm proximal operator) is notoriously difficult to accelerate on modern GPUs, and the addition of low-rank and sparse operations (Lv + Sv) can lead to high operator launch overheads during auto-regressive generation. Without latency measurements, the practical benefit for inference is unclear.

Significant training-time overheads: Performing SVD updates (even every K=40 steps) on large weight matrices scales poorly to larger model sizes (e.g., 7B+ parameters). Additionally, storing auxiliary variables (L, S, Y) for each block triples the weight memory footprint during training, which poses severe scaling challenges on memory-constrained clusters.
